causeway_guide.text: Welcome! There are about 40,000 stone columns out there, and most of them have six sides. Nobody planned that. It's cooling lava.
It all began some 60 million years ago, when molten basalt cracked as it cooled, like mud drying in a puddle.
The legend says Fionn mac Cumhaill built it to reach Scotland and fight a rival giant. The geologists have rather less fun.
It became a World Heritage Site in 1986. Wear shoes with grip. The columns are slippy and the sea is not sorry.

then.text: The Stone of Fionn is back on its plinth, and the wedding had a lovely plastic one. Thank you. The Causeway has been drawing visitors since the 1700s, and I'd like it to be there for another sixty million years.
Do remember: the stones are protected. Look, climb, photograph. Please don't pocket.
You've seen the plinth, the track, the stall, the geologist, Bushmills, the caterer, the run sheet, the events manager and that tablecloth. That's the lot. Who is it?

else.text: Still gathering? Good. Detectives who rush end up apologising to geologists.
Check the Casebook in your Fieldbook for the next lead. Come back when you've followed every lead.
Nuala Boyle, ranger. I've worked here eleven years and never lost a stone. Until this morning.
The Stone of Fionn was a loose basalt column that lives on that plinth for visitors to touch for luck. Sixty kilos, give or take a sermon. Someone has taken it overnight.

I have four people I'd like you to look at. A keyring seller, a geologist, a B&B owner in Bushmills, and, well, whoever else turns up. Ask around, look at things, and write it down. A wrong name will cost you standing.
Case opened: The Stone That Walked.
